nameStory: The white-banded fishing spider earned its name from the distinctive pale stripes that wrap around its dark body like bands, combined with its remarkable fishing abilities. Like other fishing spiders, it literally hunts at the water's edge, using the surface tension to detect prey ripples and even diving underwater to catch small fish and tadpoles.
description: The white-banded fishing spider is a large, semi-aquatic hunter that prowls the edges of ponds and streams throughout New England. This impressive spider sports a dark brown to grayish body decorated with striking white or cream-colored bands that give it its common name. They're substantial spiders that can span several inches across when their legs are extended, making them one of the more noticeable arachnids you might encounter near water.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for the diagnostic white or pale cream bands that contrast sharply against the dark brown or gray body - these bands are cleaner and more defined than the mottled patterns of other fishing spiders

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Watch for spiders sitting motionless at the water's edge with front legs touching the surface, or seemingly walking on water without breaking through - they feel surprisingly light if disturbed

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Notice the robust, somewhat flattened body that feels solid and dense compared to web-building spiders, with long legs that spread wide for water surface tension

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: These are notably large spiders - females can be quite impressive with their legs spanning 3-4 inches, while males are somewhat smaller but still substantial

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight eyes arranged in two curved rows, giving them excellent vision for hunting - they'll often turn to watch you as you approach

habitat: White-banded fishing spiders inhabit the margins of slow-moving streams, ponds, marshes, and wetlands throughout New England's lowlands and valleys. They prefer areas with overhanging vegetation or fallen logs where they can retreat quickly, and are most commonly found where the water is relatively clean and supports healthy populations of small fish, tadpoles, and aquatic insects.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from overwintering spots and become active as water temperatures rise, often seen basking in sunny spots along pond edges in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most easily observed hunting and mating, with females carrying large, round egg sacs that look like gray pearls attached to their spinnerets.
seasonality.fall: Spiderlings disperse from their mothers and adults prepare for winter, still active on warm days but beginning to seek sheltered overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate under logs, bark, or in rock crevices near water, completely inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: These spiders can dive underwater and stay submerged for up to 30 minutes by trapping a silvery air bubble around their abdomen with special water-repelling hairs - essentially carrying their own scuba tank made of air!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the dark fishing spider, but the white-banded has those distinctive clean white bands while the dark fishing spider shows more mottled, less contrasting patterns. Memory trick: 'White-banded' literally describes what you see - clear white bands, not fuzzy patterns.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'fishing spiders,' they don't actually fish with webs or lines like human anglers - the name comes from their ability to catch fish and aquatic prey with their bare legs and fangs, more like a heron than an angler.
compareHints: The white-banded fishing spider stands out from its fishing spider relatives by having the most clearly defined white bands - the dark fishing spider has more subdued, mottled markings, while the striped fishing spider shows yellowish stripes rather than bright white bands. The six-spotted fishing spider has distinctive spots rather than continuous bands, making the white-banded's clean striping pattern quite distinctive among New England's fishing spiders.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the striped fishing spider and six-spotted fishing spider which are typically found near water and have more contrasting markings, the dark fishing spider has subtler coloration and lives almost exclusively on trees.

Among New England's fishing spiders, the Striped Fishing Spider is distinguished by its pale brown coloration with prominent light stripes, while the Dark Fishing Spider is much darker and larger, and the Six-spotted Fishing Spider has distinctive white spots instead of stripes.
The six-spotted fishing spider is distinguished from its close relative the Dark Fishing Spider by its characteristic six light spots versus the Dark Fishing Spider's white side stripes.
Among New England's fishing spiders, the Banded Fishing Spider is distinguished by its bold, regular light bands across a dark body.
Among New England's fishing spiders, striatus has the most clearly defined striped patterns - other species like the dark fishing spider have more mottled or spotted appearances.
